S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.

subtypes.Persecutory Delusions: The false belief that one is being harmed or monitored by other people or organizations.
subtypes.Referential Delusions: The conviction that ordinary events, remarks, or behaviors have specific relevance to oneself.
subtypes.Grandiose Delusions: The false belief that one possesses special abilities, power, or fame.
subtypes.Erotomanic Delusions: The false belief that another person is in love with or has affection for them.
subtypes.Nihilistic Delusions: A destructive or negative conviction that the world is ending or that a major catastrophe will occur.
subtypes.Somatic Delusions: The baseless conviction that there is a serious abnormality with one's body or organs.
subtypes.Jealous Delusions: The conviction that one's spouse or romantic partner is being unfaithful without sufficient evidence.

S023.name: Negative_Symptoms
S023.description: A state where emotions, motivation, speech, or social interest that should normally be present are diminished or lost.

subtypes.Diminished Emotional Expression: A state of reduced emotional expression in facial expressions, eye contact, intonation of speech, and movements.
subtypes.Avolition: A decrease in motivated self-initiated purposeful activities.
subtypes.Alogia: A state where the quantity of spontaneous speech is significantly reduced.
subtypes.Anhedonia: A decrease in the ability to experience pleasure or interest in enjoyable activities.
subtypes.Asociality: A state where interest in social activities or interpersonal relationships is significantly reduced.

symptom.disease_info: Schizophrenia is a chronic psychotic disorder characterized by a combination of positive symptoms (such as delusions and hallucinations), negative symptoms (such as diminished emotional expression, motivation, and social engagement), and cognitive deficits, with functional decline lasting at least six months and active-phase symptoms for at least one month. Onset typically occurs in late adolescence to early adulthood, often with a prodromal period of subtle social withdrawal, decline in functioning, and odd thinking before clear psychotic symptoms emerge. The course is usually relapsing and remitting or steadily progressive, and long-term disability is closely tied to the burden of negative and cognitive symptoms rather than the intensity of positive symptoms alone. It is distinguished from mood disorders with psychotic features by the persistence of psychotic symptoms outside of mood episodes and from brief or substance-induced psychoses by its duration, functional deterioration, and lack of full return to premorbid functioning.

patient.personality: Carla is a meticulous, routine-driven designer who prefers quiet, solitary work, takes pride in preserving historic details, and keeps a small, trusted circle of collaborators.
patient.stressor: A little over two years ago, Carla and her husband decided to wind down her independent design practice in anticipation of partial retirement, shifting from a full roster of historic renovation projects to only a few select clients. This transition disrupted the daily structure she had maintained for decades—site visits, vendor meetings, and design reviews were replaced by long, unstructured days at home that she initially tried to fill with gardening, reading, and historical society work. Gradually, however, she stopped initiating new projects, let household paperwork and bills pile up in a way that was uncharacteristic for her, and began declining invitations from her volunteer group, spending more and more time alone in her craft room without actually working on her knitting or quilting. Her husband grew concerned when she seemed emotionally flat during family gatherings, no longer showed excitement about design topics, and repeatedly abandoned small home projects halfway, prompting him to encourage a psychiatric evaluation because he felt the change in her engagement and motivation had persisted for years and was affecting both her home life and remaining professional commitments.
patient.chief_complaint: I’ve slowly lost the motivation and interest to do my design work or hobbies, and I just feel like I’m going through the motions most days.

S019.name: Delusions
S019.description: Fixed beliefs that do not change easily, even in the face of contradictory evidence.
S019.manifestation: Over the past couple of years I’ve become convinced that some of my old clients and the folks at the historical society are quietly working together to monitor what I do at home—like when I see a city truck pause in front of our house or notice certain words in the preservation newsletter, it feels like they’re sending me messages about whether I’m living up to their standards, even though my husband insists it’s all just coincidence.

S023.name: Negative_Symptoms
S023.description: A state where emotions, motivation, speech, or social interest that should normally be present are diminished or lost.
S023.manifestation: These days I wake up, sit at the kitchen table with my coffee, and just stare at my old project binders or my knitting basket without any real urge to open them or call anyone, and even when my husband or the kids share good news or ask my opinion about something design-related, I hear myself giving short, flat answers and I just can’t seem to feel the enthusiasm or get myself moving like I used to.
